title: The prime-counting function is unbounded
statement: For every k there is an n with k <= pi'(n): the prime-counting function takes arbitrarily large values. This is Euclid's theorem in counting form.

formal.statement: theorem Nat.primeCounting'_unbounded : ((x0 : AxNat) -> Exists.{1} AxNat (fun (x1 : AxNat) => AxNat.le x0 (AxNat.primeCounting' x1)))

evidence.checker_command: test "$(cargo run -q -p axeyum-lean-kernel --example nat_theorem_inventory -- 'Nat.primeCounting'_unbounded' 2>/dev/null | grep -xFc 'Nat.primeCounting'_unbounded	1	((x0 : AxNat) -> Exists.{1} AxNat (fun (x1 : AxNat) => AxNat.le x0 (AxNat.primeCounting' x1)))')" -ge 1
evidence.notes: Induction on k. The base takes the witness 0 and `Nat.zero_le`. The step eliminates the hypothesis' witness n, takes a prime p > n from `Nat.exists_prime_gt`, and uses the witness succ p: pi'(succ p) = succ (pi'(p)) >= succ (pi'(n)) >= succ k. The first equality is `countRange_succ_of_true`, which needs `Eq Bool (isPrime p) true` -- and that is exactly where `F:nat-is-prime-eq-true-of-prime` is spent. Without it the two halves do not meet and this statement is not reachable from anything else in the prelude.

evidence.supports: axiom_footprint: [] -- the Nat prelude's trusted surface is empty
evidence.notes: `nat_axiom_inventory` bounds the footprint by enumerating the whole trusted surface: a theorem cannot depend on a trusted declaration the environment does not contain. All three kinds are covered -- counting `Declaration::Axiom` alone would not suffice, because `Opaque` has no proof body and `Quotient` admits `Quot.sound`. The module's own test `the_prime_counting_shelf_is_admitted_and_axiom_free` additionally asserts `Environment::contains` BEFORE reading the footprint, because `axiom_footprint` returns an empty set for a name that was never declared.

prior_art.what: Elements, Book IX, Proposition 20 (the set form)
prior_art.attribution: standard textbook attribution; this lane did not consult the primary source

notes: `F:nat-exists-prime-gt` already says the primes are unbounded as a SET. This says the prime-counting FUNCTION is unbounded, which is the form every Chebyshev-style estimate is compared against, and it is the first statement about `Nat.primeCounting'` that is not also true of `Nat.countRange` at an arbitrary predicate. It is a lower bound with no rate: it says nothing about how large n must be for pi'(n) to reach k. A rate is what Chebyshev's bounds supply, and those did not land -- see ADR-1655 for the measured obstruction.
